source_refs.note: Topic 11.3, printed pages 245-246: blood pressure, systolic and diastolic pressure, the sphygmomanometer, baroreceptors, ADH and ANH.

blocks.text: Blood pressure is the measure of the force exerted by the blood against the inner walls of the blood vessels. This force keeps blood flowing from the heart to the entire capillary network. Although such pressure occurs throughout the vascular system, the term most commonly refers to the systemic arterial blood pressure, which is highest in the aorta and gradually reduces in the systemic arteries. The walls of the arteries are elastic, and the flow of blood creates a rhythmical throbbing of the arteries, the pulse.

Arterial blood pressure rises and falls with the phases of the cardiac cycle. When the ventricles contract (ventricular systole) the heart forces blood into the pulmonary arteries and aorta and the pressure in these arteries rises sharply; the maximum pressure during ventricular systole is the systolic pressure, 120 mm Hg in a normal young adult. When the ventricles relax (diastole) the arterial pressure drops; the lowest pressure that remains in the arteries before the next ventricular contraction is the diastolic pressure, 75 to 85 mm Hg in a normal young adult. Conventionally the readings are expressed as 120/80. The sphygmomanometer is used for the manual measurement of systolic and diastolic pressures; in it the rise and fall of a mercury column shows the readings.

Pressure receptors, the baroreceptors, are present in the carotid arteries (which supply the head and brain) and the aortic arch (the portion of the aorta that bends between the ascending and descending aorta). When blood pressure falls, the baroreceptors activate sensory neurons that send information to the brain, and the control centre in the brain reacts by increasing the rate and force of contraction of the heart and by causing vasoconstriction in the arterioles; both changes restore blood pressure to normal.

The long-term regulation of blood pressure is done through hormones, which regulate the volume of blood by affecting the reabsorption of water and salt in the kidneys. When blood volume and pressure fall, special receptors in the brain create thirst and stimulate the posterior pituitary gland to secrete antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH stimulates the kidneys to retain more water in the blood, excreting less in the urine, which restores the blood volume and ultimately the pressure; ADH also constricts the arterioles, which raises arterial pressure. The walls of the right atrium contain endocrine cells that secrete atrial natriuretic hormone (ANH): when the atrium is stretched by an increased blood volume it secretes ANH, which speeds up the excretion of salts and water in the urine and so lowers the blood volume and pressure.

blocks.caption: Systolic and diastolic pressure, and how blood pressure is regulated (original diagram after Figure 11.17).
blocks.long_description: Each ventricular systole drives arterial pressure up to the systolic value, 120 mm Hg in a healthy young adult, and each diastole lets it fall to the diastolic value of 75 to 85 mm Hg, written as 120/80 and measured with a sphygmomanometer. In the short term, baroreceptors in the carotid arteries and aortic arch tell the brain when pressure falls, and the brain raises the rate and force of the heartbeat and constricts the arterioles. In the long term, hormones adjust blood volume: ADH from the posterior pituitary makes the kidneys keep water and constricts arterioles when volume is low, and ANH from the stretched right atrium makes them excrete salt and water when volume is high.
